This practical is based on the online chapter [“Confounding adjustment using propensity score methods”](https://smartdata-analysis-and-statistics.github.io/comparative-effectiveness/chapter_06.html), which complements the material in *Comparative Effectiveness and Personalized Medicine Research Using Real-World Data* (pp. 99–123). The book chapter is by Tammy Jiang, Gabrielle Simoneau, Changyu Shen, Fabio Pellegrini, and Carl de Moor.

::: {.callout-note title="How to use this practical"}
Complete the tasks and discuss the questions before opening the [worked solution](chapter3_practical1_solution.qmd). All five practicals use the same simulated cohort and treatment comparison.
:::

# Introduction

This first practical compares the baseline characteristics of patients receiving DMT1 and DMT0, fits a propensity-score model, and assesses overlap. A propensity score (PS) is the probability of receiving the treatment of interest conditional on measured baseline covariates. It describes treatment assignment; it is not the probability of a good outcome.

These practicals use the `generate_data()` simulator supplied for this work, with the same multiple-sclerosis covariates, treatment, relapse-count outcome, follow-up time, and `Iscore` structure shown in the reference chapter. The simulator documentation says treatment is randomized, but its implementation assigns treatment using a logistic model of baseline covariates. That implementation is observational, which makes it suitable for teaching propensity-score adjustment. The generated cohort is saved once as an RDS file and reused in every practical.

## Learning objectives

By completing this practical, you will be able to:

- summarize and compare baseline characteristics by treatment group using appropriate descriptive measures;
- use standardized mean differences to describe measured-covariate imbalance without baseline hypothesis tests;
- estimate a propensity score using logistic regression with prespecified pretreatment covariates; and
- inspect propensity-score overlap and explain why treatment-prediction accuracy alone does not establish a suitable adjustment model.

# 1. Prepare and compare the baseline data


```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "tableone", "cobalt", "MatchIt", "marginaleffects"))
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(cobalt)
data_file <- if (file.exists("data/chapter3_ps_data.rds")) {
  "data/chapter3_ps_data.rds"
} else {
  "Chapter_3/data/chapter3_ps_data.rds"
}
dat <- readRDS(data_file)
ps_formula <- treatment ~ age + female + prevDMTefficacy +
  premedicalcost + prerelapse_num + numSymptoms
```

The outcome `y` is the number of observed relapses and `years` is follow-up time. The generator's treatment-allocation model uses age, sex, previous DMT efficacy, prior relapse count, premedical cost, and symptom count. Include these measured baseline variables in the propensity-score model. In a real study, justify the adjustment set from subject-matter knowledge and a causal diagram rather than selecting variables by statistical significance.

**Tasks:**

1. Inspect the data dimensions, variable names, treatment counts, and missing values.
```{r}
#| eval: false
dim(dat)
str(dat)
table(dat$treatment)
colSums(is.na(dat))
```

2. Create a baseline characteristics table comparing DMT1 and DMT0, similar to the table in the reference chapter. Include all six baseline covariates in the PS model, report categorical variables as n (%) and continuous variables as mean (SD), and show the sample size in each treatment group. Do not add baseline hypothesis tests.
```{r}
#| eval: false
baseline_vars <- c("age", "female", "prevDMTefficacy",
                   "premedicalcost", "prerelapse_num", "numSymptoms")
categorical_vars <- c("female", "prevDMTefficacy", "numSymptoms")

baseline_table <- tableone::CreateTableOne(
  vars = baseline_vars,
  strata = "treatment",
  data = dat,
  factorVars = categorical_vars,
  test = FALSE
)

print(baseline_table)
```

3. Compare the six baseline covariates between treatment groups using standardized mean differences (SMDs) to describe imbalance; do not use hypothesis tests to select covariates.
```{r}
#| eval: false
bal.tab(ps_formula, data = dat, un = TRUE)
```

# 2. Methods based on the propensity score

The propensity score (PS) summarizes each patient's probability of receiving treatment given measured baseline characteristics. It can be used in several ways to make treated and untreated groups more comparable. In this practical, you will inspect the baseline data and estimate the PS. The next practicals show how to apply it using matching (Practical 2), stratification (Practical 3), weighting (Practical 4), and regression adjustment for the propensity score (Practical 5). Each method has different assumptions and diagnostics; those will be introduced alongside the method where they are used.

4. Fit the supplied logistic treatment model and calculate a predicted treatment probability for each participant.
```{r}
#| eval: false
ps_fit <- glm(ps_formula, data = dat, family = binomial())
dat$ps <- predict(ps_fit, type = "response")
summary(ps_fit)
```

5. Plot the propensity-score distributions by treatment and report the range in each group.
```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(dat, aes(x = ps, fill = treatment)) +
  geom_histogram(position = "identity", alpha = .45, bins = 30) +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(DMT0 = "#80c42b", DMT1 = "#26476b"),
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Probability of Treatment", y = "Count",
       title = "Propensity Score Distribution by Treatment Group") +
  theme_minimal()
dat %>% group_by(treatment) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), min = min(ps), median = median(ps), max = max(ps))
```
